props.title: Shake Hands with the Devil

sections.content: Shake Hands with the Devil delivers a haunting portrayal of Canadian General Roméo Dallaire's experience during the 1994 Rwandan genocide. The film, based on Dallaire's memoir, stands among the most devastating accounts of UN peacekeeping failures, alongside Hotel Rwanda (2004) and Sometimes in April (2005). Director Roger Spottiswoode and actor Roy Dupuis capture Dallaire's psychological torment as he witnesses the systematic slaughter of 800,000 Tutsis while his pleas for UN intervention go ignored. This adaptation provides a crucial perspective on institutional paralysis during humanitarian crises.

sections.content: The film's power lies in its unflinching examination of Western complicity through inaction. Like The Killing Fields (1984) and The Year of Living Dangerously (1982), it forces viewers to confront how international observers become unwitting participants in mass atrocity. Dallaire's post-traumatic stress disorder receives careful attention, prefiguring later films about peacekeepers' mental health like War Story (2014) and A Perfect Day (2015).

Documentary elements strengthen the narrative, incorporating actual footage and survivor testimonies similar to Shooting Dogs (2005) and 100 Days (2001). The film's structure, moving between Dallaire's present-day trauma and flashbacks to Rwanda, creates a devastating portrait of how genocide's psychological impact reverberates long after the killing ends. sections.content: Shake Hands with the Devil influenced later films about international intervention in mass atrocity, including The Whistleblower (2010) and No Man's Land (2001). Its focus on bureaucratic failure and individual moral responsibility established a template for examining institutional culpability in crisis situations, seen again in films like The Last King of Scotland (2006) and Beasts of No Nation (2015).
